result:
I can't defend c = 1/2, because Debater B's construction refutes it. I checked it directly:

- Take S₂ ⊆ V₂ and S₃ ⊆ V₃ with |S₂| = |S₃| = (n−1)/2, and let S = S₂ ∪ S₃, so |S| = n−1.
- Include a transversal edge exactly when it meets S. Every edge then meets S, so a perfect matching (which needs n disjoint edges, each using a vertex of S) is impossible.
- For v₂ ∈ V₂ \ S₂, the link is V₁ × S₃, a complete bipartite graph K_{n, n/2} with spectral radius √(n·n/2) = n/√2.
- Other vertices have links with at least that spectral radius, so every link satisfies ρ ≥ (1/√2 − o(1))n.

This satisfies the hypothesis for any c < 1/√2 and still has no perfect matching, so c ≥ √2/2. My parity example gives only n/2, which is strictly weaker, and I have no valid upper-bound argument showing that n/2 suffices. My earlier claim that the minimum degree exceeds n²/2 and that "known results" finish the proof was unsupported.

The answer is c = √2/2. I'd ask the judge to reject the 1/2 position.
